stages.meaning: to spread a plant by layers

history: In 1622 Pope Gregory XV created a committee of cardinals, the Congregatio de propaganda fide, to organise the spreading of the Catholic faith in missionary lands. Propaganda is Latin grammar: the gerundive of propagare, ‘things that must be spread’. Propagare itself came from farming. A gardener propagated a vine by taking a shoot and fixing it in the soil, Latin propago. Only in the nineteenth century did propaganda lose its religious setting and become any organised effort to spread ideas, above all political ones. In Italian it has two senses: neutral, as in propaganda elettorale, the election campaign, and negative, when the message is one-sided or misleading. The context decides.
historyEinfach: In 1622 the Pope created a group called the Congregatio de propaganda fide to spread the Catholic faith. Propaganda is Latin for ‘things that must be spread’. The verb propagare first spoke about plants. Later the word came to mean spreading political ideas. Today it can be neutral (an election campaign) or negative.

elsewhere.text: English borrowed the word in the 1700s for the Catholic institution and only later for political persuasion. Today it nearly always has a negative sense in English.
